title: Can AI Agents Really Shift Chip Design Left?
gist: Roundtable (Synopsys, Hiveware, Silvaco, Axiomise) on agentic AI in chip design: agents are proliferating per tool/flow step into a hierarchical 'onion of agents', but no one yet knows how to orchestrate them coherently, token costs may favor big companies, and the decisive bottleneck is siloed proprietary design data and decades of uncodified engineering expertise.

themes.theme: Agent orchestration as the next EDA methodology

insights.claim: Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari argues that combining AI agents across the chip flow will become a new industry methodology direction comparable to UVM, but that nobody today really knows how that combination will work.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Watch for a standard/methodology for multi-agent EDA flows; whoever defines it (vendor or consortium) gains lock-in.
insights.quote: I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work.
insights.locator: SE: If AI agents are modifying code

insights.claim: Synopsys' Frank Schirrmeister describes agentic chip design as an 'onion of agents': each sub-flow (virtual prototyping, formal, simulation, emulation, prototyping) gets its own localized agent, then orchestrating agents sit on top and connect to the front end.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Value accrues to whoever owns the orchestration layer on top of point-tool agents, favoring broad-portfolio EDA vendors.
insights.quote: This is an onion of agents, with more and more layers on top.

insights.claim: According to Schirrmeister, EDA vendors all claim 'Level 5' agentic autonomy, which is true only within the scope of each tool's narrow operating domain rather than end-to-end.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Discount vendor 'Level 5' autonomy marketing; ask about cross-domain orchestration, not single-tool autonomy.
insights.quote: EDA vendors are all saying we have Level 5 stuff, and there’s truth to that within the scope of the operating domain.

insights.claim: Silvaco's Jack Berg says the industry will build and iteratively improve agents at each level with a Level 5 agent orchestrating the whole, which he sees as the only way for agents to replace large groups of engineers doing grunt work.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Signals an expected labor-substitution story for EDA customers; watch for headcount/productivity claims tied to agent deployments.
insights.quote: That’s the only way in which you’re going to get agents to learn and replace large groups of engineers doing the grunt work that’s necessary here.
insights.locator: Berg: You’ve got levels of agents

insights.claim: Hiveware's Ronen Laviv speculates that AI may develop its own language producing synthesizable SystemVerilog RTL, reducing reliance on UVM and software in co-simulation, which slows emulation; he suggests UVM might not stay forever.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Potential long-term disruption to verification methodology and emulation usage models (hardware emulator demand could rise if software overhead drops).
insights.locator: Laviv: One of the challenges with emulation

insights.claim: Darbari cites Nvidia's head of GPU saying at DVCon U.S. that formal verification is replacing, or will replace, simulation.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A leading chip buyer favoring formal over simulation would shift verification tool spend toward formal vendors like Axiomise.
insights.quote: The formal is replacing simulation, or is going to replace simulation.

themes.theme: Cost of tokens and big-company advantage

insights.claim: Darbari questions whether small chip companies can afford the token costs of running full agentic flows and believes only big companies will be able to, noting some large firms say they have written no code themselves and run everything via agents.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agentic EDA may widen the gap between large and small chip designers; watch token pricing and EDA AI licensing models.
insights.quote: I have a feeling that only the big companies will be able to afford this.
insights.locator: Darbari: The ones running the product.

insights.claim: Schirrmeister counters that smaller, previously difficult designs will benefit from agentic flows, but that building an Nvidia competitor still cannot be done 'out of your garage' and requires a big company.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: AI agents lower barriers for small designs but do not erode the moat of leading-edge AI chip incumbents.
insights.quote: If you want to be an Nvidia competitor, you still cannot do this out of your garage.

insights.claim: Berg says agentic flows must feed manufacturing constraints back into the functional specification to improve the probability of manufacturability, and without early multi-physics checks a design will be 'dead on arrival in manufacturing'.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Opportunity for TCAD/multi-physics simulation vendors (e.g., Silvaco) if agents need early physical-effects prediction.
insights.quote: Yes, and without that, it will be dead on arrival in manufacturing.

insights.claim: Laviv says AI handles about 80% of chip design challenges well, but the remainder depends on skills of engineers with ~30 years of experience; one discussion identified 250 distinct skills across power, emulation and verification that AI lacks today.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The last-20% expertise gap is the key adoption limiter; firms that capture tacit engineering knowledge gain an edge.
insights.quote: AI is doing a great job on, say, 80% of the challenges.
insights.locator: Laviv: AI is doing a great

insights.claim: Laviv argues the industry must figure out how to gather decades of design expertise hidden inside companies such as Apple, Qualcomm and Intel before agent-to-agent flows can work fully.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Large incumbents' proprietary know-how is a strategic asset in agentic EDA; it is not readily available to tool vendors.
insights.quote: all the decades of experience that is hidden in Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel
insights.locator: Laviv: AI is doing a great

insights.claim: Berg uses AlphaFold, credited in the 2024 chemistry Nobel Prize after 50 years of protein-folding work, as proof of concept that AI prediction will happen in semiconductors; Laviv rebuts that protein data is open while chip data is not.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Data openness, not model capability, may be the gating factor for AI in chip design.
insights.quote: The difference is that with proteins, everything is open.

themes.theme: Data silos and the vendor vs. user race

insights.claim: Darbari says many agentic AI startups lack field experience and are building what customers do not want, so big chip consumers are building their own agentic tools using years of their own data.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Headwind for EDA AI startups; large customers in-sourcing AI tooling caps vendor TAM.
insights.quote: A lot of agentic AI companies lack the field experience of having seen these problems firsthand, so what they’re building is not what the consumer wants.
insights.locator: SE: If AI agents are modifying code

insights.claim: Citing Simon Davidmann, Schirrmeister frames the 'big three' EDA vendors as owning base tools on which they build agent stacks, while AI-native entrants must learn EDA first and lack access to the design data, which users hold.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Incumbent EDA vendors' base-tool ownership is a moat against AI-native challengers.
insights.quote: People who know AI well found EDA. But they need to learn EDA first, rather than the other way around, and they don’t have access to the data they need.
insights.locator: Schirrmeister: Yes. Where does the data

insights.claim: Samsung built its own LLM fed with data from a fast classic engine, SoC simulator and emulator to optimize network-on-chip quality of service, keeping that company data in-house.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Example of a major chipmaker in-sourcing AI on proprietary data rather than relying on vendor models.
insights.quote: That’s their company data, and it’s not going out to anybody.
insights.locator: Schirrmeister: Yes. Where does the data

insights.claim: Cognichip argues LLMs must be trained with real chip designs and people, which is why it hired chip designers and built chips.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: AI-EDA startups may need to generate proprietary design data themselves to compete; watch Cognichip's approach.
insights.quote: Cognichip said you need LLMs that are trained with real chip designs and people
insights.locator: Schirrmeister: Yes. Where does the data
